tldr: For articulated object manipulation (such as drawers and doors) using quadrupedal robots, the authors propose "TONAV," a framework that integrates language reasoning and adaptive control to reach manipulation-ready configurations with an action-velocity chunk policy that maintains stable contact.
hero_caption: Core concept of TONAV. Unlike conventional methods that simply stop near the target, TONAV progressively approaches a manipulation-ready configuration and achieves smooth, continuous contact manipulation via position-velocity-coupled control.
overview:
Mobile manipulation of articulated objects (objects with rotational axes or sliding mechanisms), such as closing drawers or opening cabinet doors in home environments, is an extremely challenging task for robots. Conventional systems face two major hurdles. First, existing object navigation often stops 1 to 2 meters short of the target. This leaves a "navigation-manipulation gap" where the arm cannot reach or hits its joint limits. Second, manipulation policies typically predict only joint positions. When moving along an object's constrained trajectory, this causes motion jitter, loss of contact, and tracking lag.

This paper proposes "TONAV," a unified framework that tackles both challenges. On the navigation side, it uses a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) with a Perception-Planning Chain-of-Thought (PP-CoT) to decompose the global path into subgoals. An Adaptive Approach Module (AAM) then compensates for visual latency using a Kalman filter, fine-tuning the robot base toward a "manipulation-ready configuration" where the arm can move most effectively.

On the manipulation side, the authors collect high-quality demonstration data using an Action-Velocity Teleoperation Framework (AVTF) that couples position and velocity via impedance control. Then, through Action-Velocity Chunk Learning, the policy jointly predicts future position and velocity sequences. In real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2-W with a Piper arm, TONAV demonstrated substantial performance gains: a navigation success rate of 60.00% (+33.33 to +46.67 percentage points over baselines) and a manipulation success rate of 80.00% (+33.33 to +53.33 percentage points over baselines).
contributions: Established task-oriented navigation that converges the robot base to a manipulation-ready configuration by combining MLLM-based PP-CoT with an Adaptive Approach Module (AAM) featuring visual latency compensation.
Developed a position-velocity-coupled teleoperation framework (AVTF) to reduce master-follower lag and motion inconsistency during demonstration collection.
Significantly improved the stability of sustained-contact manipulation by jointly predicting position and velocity sequences in action chunk learning with an intra-chunk motion consistency loss.

sections.heading: Reaching Is Not Enough: The Gap Between Task Navigation and Sustained Contact
sections.summary: Mobile manipulation requires both reaching a manipulation-ready base configuration and maintaining stable trajectory tracking under contact. Conventional object navigation stops too coarsely, and manipulation policies rely solely on position prediction, causing motions to fail.
sections.details:
Mobile manipulation is a foundational technology for home robots, but practical deployment faces two tightly coupled challenges.

The first challenge is "task-oriented navigation." Most existing object-search navigation methods consider a run successful if the robot reaches within 1 to 2 meters of the target. However, this often leaves the robot with the wrong orientation, too close to a drawer to unfold its arm, or too far away to reach. To complete a task, the robot base must be progressively guided into a "manipulation-ready" configuration that accounts for the arm's workspace.

The second challenge is "sustained-contact manipulation." Articulated objects, such as drawers or toilet lids, must be moved along trajectories constrained by their physical mechanisms. Action chunking (predicting sequences of actions) used in imitation learning is powerful, but most methods predict only joint positions. Relying solely on position information omits the underlying motion dynamics—specifically, at what velocity transitions should happen. This frequently leads to tracking lag, jitter at chunk boundaries, and accidental contact disengagement.

TONAV aims to break through both barriers at once by uniting MLLM-driven reasoning with adaptive approach navigation, alongside position-velocity-coupled teleoperation and chunk learning.

sections.heading: Related Work: The Divide in Navigation and Limitations of Modular Pipelines
sections.summary: Prior navigation work has been split between distant goal guidance and local fine-tuning, lacking a cohesive approach. Furthermore, base placement heuristics in mobile manipulation remain inadequate for tightly constrained articulated objects.
sections.details:
Research in robot navigation has largely been divided into two separate tiers: global goal guidance and last-mile fine-tuning.

- Goal-directed navigation: Visual-Language Navigation (VLN) and open-vocabulary exploration allow robots to follow instructions in novel environments, but their stopping points remain coarse.
- Last-mile navigation: Imitation learning, reinforcement learning, and learning graspable base placements from large-scale data have been explored. However, they lack a continuous, closed-loop mechanism linking global navigation to local fine adjustment.

Meanwhile, mobile manipulation methods that integrate base mobility with arm control are broadly categorized into end-to-end and modular approaches. End-to-end learning demands prohibitive data collection costs, making modular designs that separate navigation from manipulation more practical. Nonetheless, the heuristics used in existing modular pipelines—such as base placement scoring or grasp area sampling—struggle to meet the strict base positioning and continuous contact constraints required for articulated objects.

sections.heading: Architecture of TONAV: From Reasoning-Adaptive Navigation to Action-Velocity Chunk Learning
sections.summary: TONAV consists of an upstream navigation system and a downstream manipulation system. It positions the base using LLM reasoning (PP-CoT) and visual tracking (AAM), and enables smooth contact manipulation via position-velocity-coupled teleoperation (AVTF) and chunk learning.
sections.details:
The overall TONAV system is split into two primary branches: navigation and manipulation.

III-A Position-Velocity-Coupled Teleoperation Framework (AVTF)
Conventional teleoperation transmits only master joint angles (positions), which causes tracking lag. To solve this, AVTF estimates joint velocities $\dot{\mathbf{q}}_{t}^{m,\mathrm{ref}}$ from consecutive master positions, clips them within safe bounds, and sends both positions and velocities to the follower arm. The follower arm tracks these inputs at $220\,\mathrm{Hz}$ using an MIT-style impedance controller. By decoupling the control loop from the recording loop ($30\,\mathrm{Hz}$), the system prevents camera capture and logging from delaying low-level control, ensuring high-quality, temporally consistent demonstrations.

III-B Perception-Planning Chain-of-Thought (PP-CoT)
Generating actions directly from language instructions is prone to perceptual errors. Therefore, TONAV drives the MLLM with a two-stage prompt. The first stage (Perception) identifies the target object, landmarks, and navigable areas. The second stage (Planning) produces a visible route connecting them, outputting a sequence of subgoal instructions such as "go straight," "turn left at landmark," and "stop."

III-C Adaptive Approach Module (AAM)
An open-vocabulary detector combined with SAM2 extracts the target object's mask and calculates its 3D position in the camera frame. To compensate for camera displacement caused by SAM2 processing latency, TONAV integrates an egomotion-aware Kalman filter. From the filtered target position, it computes the horizontal image center error $e^u_t$ and the distance error $e^d_t$. The base switches between turning and moving straight to converge to an optimal offset distance $d^\star$ tuned to the arm's workspace.

III-D Action-Velocity Chunk Learning for Sustained Contact
The manipulation policy adopts an ACT-based CVAE. From visual features and proprioception, parallel decoders jointly predict future position chunks $\hat{\mathbf{q}}$ and velocity chunks $\hat{\dot{\mathbf{q}}}$. The loss function includes an L1 loss on actual follower joint positions $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pos}}$, a velocity supervision loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vel}}$, and a motion consistency loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{con}}$ that penalizes discrepancies between the temporal differences of predicted positions and the predicted velocities. This eliminates jitter at chunk boundaries and greatly stabilizes pushing and pulling along constrained paths.

sections.heading: Real-World Experiments: Large Gains in Navigation and Contact Manipulation
sections.summary: Using a quadruped robot (Go2-W) and a Piper arm, TONAV was evaluated across three tasks: closing a drawer, turning on a desk lamp, and lowering a toilet lid. TONAV achieved a 60.00% navigation success rate and an 80.00% manipulation success rate, outperforming baseline methods by wide margins.
sections.details:
Real-world hardware experiments were conducted using a Unitree Go2-W (wheeled-quadruped robot) and two Piper arms (one teleoperation master and one onboard follower).

Quantitative Evaluation (Navigation):
Evaluating navigation success across three tasks (Close Drawer, Turn On Lamp, Lower Toilet Lid), TONAV achieved an overall success rate of $60.00\%$. This significantly outperformed existing VLN methods, including StreamVLN ($13.33\%$) and InternNav ($26.67\%$). While baselines could approach the vicinity of objects, they frequently failed because incorrect base orientation or distance placed the target outside the arm's reach.
In ablation studies, removing PP-CoT dropped the success rate of Qwen-3.7-Max from $60.00\%$ to $26.67\%$, confirming that chain-of-thought subgoal decomposition is essential.

Quantitative Evaluation (Manipulation):
Manipulation performance was evaluated starting from manipulation-ready configurations. Conventional ACT and Diffusion Policy (DP), which predict position only, achieved a success rate of just $13.33\%$. In contrast, TONAV trained on position-velocity teleoperated data with velocity supervision and consistency loss reached an $80.00\%$ success rate. Even when trained on data collected without position-velocity control, TONAV achieved $53.33\%$, demonstrating the architectural benefit as well as its synergy with high-quality demonstrations.

Qualitative Evaluation and Trajectory Analysis:
Comparing joint angle trajectories (Figure F8), ACT and DP exhibited severe joint angle oscillations (jitter) due to target object reaction forces and chunk transitions. In contrast, TONAV produced smooth, continuous curves. In continuous-contact tasks like lowering a toilet lid, the end-effector pushed through to completion without slipping off the target.

sections.heading: Conclusion and Outlook: Toward a New Standard for Contact-Rich Mobile Manipulation
sections.summary: TONAV demonstrates the power of combining staged task-oriented navigation with action-velocity chunk learning. Future improvements are expected through the integration of tactile sensors and better generalization across unseen furniture arrangements.
sections.details:
This paper presented TONAV, an end-to-end framework addressing navigation through contact manipulation for articulated objects using a quadrupedal mobile manipulator.

The key to its success lies in bridging two capabilities: a two-stage navigation approach that guides the base specifically to manipulation-ready configurations, and chunk learning that models not just where to go (position) but also how to transition (velocity). This unified approach mitigates hardware tracking lag and motion jitter, enabling stable, sustained-contact interaction.

For future work, the authors highlight incorporating tactile sensing to better adapt to external disturbances, as well as expanding geometric generalization across diverse room layouts and initial robot placements.

takeaways: Getting near an object is fundamentally different from reaching an actionable configuration; a last-mile alignment mechanism tailored to the arm's workspace is critical.
Jointly predicting and supervising velocity alongside position in action chunk learning—enforced by a motion consistency loss—dramatically cuts down tracking lag and jitter in contact tasks.
Coupling position and velocity through impedance tracking right from the teleoperation stage produces high-quality, temporally consistent demonstration data.
limitations: Haptic or tactile feedback is not currently integrated to react immediately to external disturbances or unexpected contact force variations.
Geometric generalization over long-horizon tasks and unseen environments with markedly different furniture arrangements requires further validation.
